course.title: Chemistry II: Reactions & Organic Basics
course.description: A second pass through chemistry focused on what reactions do — how to balance them, how fast they go, where they settle, and the acids, energy, and carbon compounds behind them. Structure adapted from OpenStax Chemistry 2e (CC BY 4.0). Extends the earlier Introduction to Chemistry course.

questions.prompt: Balance it: __H2 + __O2 → __H2O. The coefficients are…
questions.explanation: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O balances 4 H and 2 O on each side — see 'Types of reactions & balancing'.

questions.prompt: The reaction CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O is a…
questions.explanation: A hydrocarbon burning in O2 to give CO2 and H2O is combustion.

questions.prompt: Raising the temperature generally makes a reaction's rate…
questions.explanation: Higher temperature means more frequent, more energetic collisions — see 'Reaction rates'.

questions.prompt: At chemical equilibrium, the forward and reverse reaction rates are…
questions.explanation: Equilibrium is dynamic: forward rate = reverse rate, so concentrations stop changing.

questions.prompt: For an exothermic reaction, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium…
questions.explanation: Added heat is a 'stress' the system relieves by running the endothermic (reverse) direction — Le Chatelier.

questions.prompt: A solution with [H+] = 1×10⁻³ M has a pH of…
questions.explanation: pH = -log(1×10⁻³) = 3 — see 'Acids, bases & pH'.

questions.prompt: Which quantity measures the heat released or absorbed at constant pressure?
questions.explanation: Enthalpy change ΔH tracks heat at constant pressure; negative ΔH means heat is released.

questions.prompt: The general molecular formula for an alkane is…
questions.explanation: Saturated (single-bond) hydrocarbons follow CnH2n+2 — see 'Intro to organic chemistry'.

lessons.title: Types of reactions & balancing equations
lessons.grammar_note: A balanced equation changes coefficients (the big numbers in front), never subscripts.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Recognize the major reaction types and balance a chemical equation by conserving atoms. Warm-up: in the equation 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O, what do the numbers 2 in front actually count — molecules or atoms inside a molecule?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Atoms are never created or destroyed in a reaction (conservation of mass), so both sides of an equation must show the *same count of each element*. You balance by adjusting *coefficients* — the whole-number multipliers in front of each formula — while leaving subscripts alone. Most reactions fall into a few families: combination/synthesis (A + B → AB), decomposition (AB → A + B), single replacement (A + BC → AC + B), double replacement (AB + CD → AD + CB, often forming a precipitate), and combustion (a hydrocarbon + O2 → CO2 + H2O). Worked start: for 2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl, count Na (2 = 2) and Cl (2 = 2) — balanced, and it's a synthesis.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Combustion of propane: C3H8 + O2 → CO2 + H2O. Balance C first (3 CO2), then H (4 H2O = 8 H), then O last: right side has 3×2 + 4×1 = 10 O, so put 5 in front of O2. Result: C3H8 + 5O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O. Check: C 3=3, H 8=8, O 10=10. Single replacement: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2 — H is 2=2, Cl is 2=2. Decomposition: 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2 — H 4=4, O 4=4. Precipitation (double replacement): AgNO3 + NaCl → AgCl↓ + NaNO3 — every element 1=1.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Balance each (give the coefficients in order): (1) __Al + __O2 → __Al2O3, (2) __N2 + __H2 → __NH3, (3) __Fe + __O2 → __Fe2O3, (4) __CH4 + __O2 → __CO2 + __H2O, (5) name the type of Mg + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2. Answers: (1) 4, 3, 2; (2) 1, 3, 2; (3) 4, 3, 2; (4) 1, 2, 1, 2; (5) single replacement.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: changing a subscript (writing H2O2 instead of putting a 2 in front of H2O) to 'make it balance' — that changes the substance. Mistake: forgetting oxygen appears in two products in combustion, so balance it last. Exit: (a) In 4Al + 3O2 → 2Al2O3, how many oxygen atoms are on each side? (b) Which family is 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2? Answers: 6 on each side; decomposition.

lessons.title: Reaction rates: how fast, and why
lessons.grammar_note: Rate order: rate = k[A]ⁿ. First order (n=1) scales ×, second order (n=2) scales ×².

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name the factors that change a reaction's rate and use a simple rate law to predict how rate responds to concentration. Warm-up: two pieces of the same metal react with acid — one is a solid lump, one is powder. Which reacts faster, and why?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Reactions happen when particles *collide* with enough energy (the *activation energy*, Ea) and the right orientation. Anything that raises collision frequency or energy speeds the reaction: higher *concentration*, higher *temperature*, greater *surface area*, and adding a *catalyst* (which lowers Ea without being used up). A *rate law* captures the concentration dependence: rate = k[A]ⁿ, where k is the rate constant and n is the reaction order. Worked start: for a first-order reaction (n = 1), doubling [A] doubles the rate; the rate scales in direct proportion.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Second order, rate = k[A]²: with k = 2 M⁻¹s⁻¹ and [A] = 3 M, rate = 2 × (3)² = 18 M/s. Now double [A] to 6 M: rate = 2 × (6)² = 72 M/s — that's 4× larger, because 2² = 4. A catalyst example: it opens a lower-Ea pathway, so more collisions clear the energy barrier, but it is regenerated and appears unchanged at the end. Temperature: a rough rule of thumb is that many reaction rates roughly double for each 10 °C rise, because a small energy boost pushes far more collisions over Ea.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: (1) For rate = k[A] (first order), if [A] triples, the rate changes by what factor? (2) For rate = k[A]², if [A] doubles, the rate changes by what factor? (3) Does a catalyst raise or lower the activation energy? (4) Compute the rate for rate = k[A]² with k = 0.5 M⁻¹s⁻¹ and [A] = 4 M. (5) Powder vs. lump of the same metal — which has more surface area and reacts faster? Answers: (1) ×3; (2) ×4; (3) lowers it; (4) 0.5 × 16 = 8 M/s; (5) the powder.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming a catalyst is consumed — it is regenerated and left over at the end. Mistake: reading the exponent as a coefficient — in rate = k[A]², doubling [A] gives 2² = 4× the rate, not 2×. Exit: (a) Name two ways to speed a reaction without changing the chemicals involved. (b) A reaction is second order in A; [A] is halved — what happens to the rate? Answers: raise temperature / increase surface area (or add a catalyst); it drops to one quarter (½² = ¼).

lessons.title: Equilibrium & Le Chatelier's principle
lessons.grammar_note: Le Chatelier: a system at equilibrium shifts to partly undo any stress you apply.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Write an equilibrium constant expression and predict the direction a reaction shifts when it is stressed. Warm-up: if the forward and reverse reactions never stop, why do the amounts of each substance hold steady at equilibrium?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Many reactions are reversible and settle into *dynamic equilibrium*, where the forward and reverse rates are equal so concentrations stay constant. The balance point is described by the *equilibrium constant*: for aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, Kc = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ / ([A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ), products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient. *Le Chatelier's principle* predicts responses to stress: add a reactant → shift toward products; remove a product → shift toward products; raise pressure (shrink volume) → shift toward the side with fewer gas moles; change temperature → treat heat as a reactant (endothermic) or product (exothermic). Worked start: for N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, Kc = [NH3]² / ([N2][H2]³).

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Compute Kc for H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI when equilibrium concentrations are [H2] = 0.10 M, [I2] = 0.10 M, [HI] = 0.80 M: Kc = [HI]² / ([H2][I2]) = (0.80)² / (0.10 × 0.10) = 0.64 / 0.010 = 64. Now the Haber reaction N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 (exothermic, ΔH < 0): add N2 → shifts right (makes more NH3); remove NH3 → shifts right; raise pressure → the left has 4 gas moles vs. 2 on the right, so it shifts right toward fewer moles; raise temperature → heat is a 'product,' so it shifts left toward reactants; add a catalyst → no shift, equilibrium is just reached sooner.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: For 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g), ΔH < 0 (exothermic), predict the shift for each stress: (1) add more O2; (2) remove SO3; (3) raise the temperature; (4) increase the pressure; (5) add a catalyst. Answers: (1) right; (2) right; (3) left (heat behaves as a product); (4) right (3 gas moles → 2, fewer on the right); (5) no shift — it reaches equilibrium faster.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking a catalyst changes the equilibrium position — it changes only the speed of reaching it, not Kc. Mistake: for pressure, comparing total molecules instead of counting *gas* moles on each side. Exit: (a) In Kc, do products go on top or bottom? (b) For an exothermic reaction, which direction does cooling it down shift the equilibrium? Answers: on top (numerator); toward products (removing heat pulls the exothermic forward reaction).

questions.prompt: Balanced correctly, C3H8 + O2 → CO2 + H2O has coefficients…
A catalyst speeds a reaction by…
questions.explanation: It provides a lower-Ea pathway and is regenerated, not consumed.

questions.prompt: For a rate law rate = k[A]², doubling [A] changes the rate by a factor of…
questions.explanation: Second order: 2² = 4.

questions.prompt: For N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, adding more N2 shifts the equilibrium…
questions.explanation: Adding a reactant pushes the system toward products (right).

questions.prompt: For aA + bB ⇌ cC, the equilibrium constant is written as…
questions.explanation: Products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient.

questions.prompt: The reaction Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2 is best classified as…
questions.explanation: One element (Zn) replaces another (H) in a compound.

lessons.title: Acids, bases & pH calculations
lessons.grammar_note: pH = -log[H+]. Each whole pH unit is a 10× change in [H+].

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Relate [H+], [OH-], and pH, and calculate pH for strong acids and bases. Warm-up: if one solution has pH 3 and another has pH 5, how many times more acidic (higher [H+]) is the first?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: An *Arrhenius acid* releases H+ in water; an *Arrhenius base* releases OH-. Water self-ionizes so that [H+][OH-] = Kw = 1.0×10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C. We compress those tiny numbers with a log scale: *pH = -log[H+]* and *pOH = -log[OH-]*, which gives the handy relation pH + pOH = 14 at 25 °C. A *strong* acid or base dissociates essentially completely, so its concentration equals the ion concentration. Worked start: for 0.001 M HCl, [H+] = 1×10⁻³ M, so pH = -log(1×10⁻³) = 3.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: 0.01 M HCl (strong acid): [H+] = 1×10⁻² M, pH = -log(10⁻²) = 2. Neutral water: [H+] = 1×10⁻⁷ M, pH = 7. 0.001 M NaOH (strong base): [OH-] = 1×10⁻³ M, so pOH = 3 and pH = 14 - 3 = 11. Going backward from pH to concentration: a solution of pH 4 has [H+] = 10⁻⁴ = 1×10⁻⁴ M. Scale intuition: pH 3 vs. pH 5 differ by 2 units, so the pH-3 solution has 10² = 100× the [H+].

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: (1) A solution has [H+] = 1×10⁻⁴ M — what is its pH? (2) 0.1 M HCl (strong) — what is its pH? (3) A solution has pH 9 — what is [H+]? (4) A strong base has [OH-] = 1×10⁻² M — what is its pH? (5) Is a solution of pH 3 acidic or basic? Answers: (1) pH = 4; (2) [H+] = 10⁻¹, pH = 1; (3) [H+] = 1×10⁻⁹ M; (4) pOH = 2, so pH = 12; (5) acidic (pH < 7).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating pH as linear — dropping from pH 5 to pH 3 is a *100×* rise in [H+], not a small one. Mistake: forgetting to convert pOH to pH for a base (find pOH first, then subtract from 14). Exit: (a) What is the pH of a 0.0001 M HCl solution? (b) A solution has pOH 6 — what is its pH? Answers: [H+] = 10⁻⁴, so pH = 4; pH = 14 - 6 = 8.

lessons.title: Intro to organic chemistry
lessons.grammar_note: Carbon forms exactly 4 bonds. Alkane/alkene/alkyne = single/double/triple C–C bonds.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Classify simple hydrocarbons and identify common functional groups. Warm-up: carbon has four valence electrons — how many covalent bonds does a carbon atom form in a stable organic molecule?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds. Carbon forms four bonds, letting it build chains and rings. *Hydrocarbons* (carbon + hydrogen only) come in three families by bond type: *alkanes* (all single bonds, CnH2n+2), *alkenes* (at least one C=C double bond, CnH2n), and *alkynes* (a C≡C triple bond, CnH2n-2). A *functional group* is a specific atom cluster that gives a molecule its characteristic reactions: *hydroxyl* (-OH, alcohols), *carboxyl* (-COOH, carboxylic acids), *amino* (-NH2, amines), and *carbonyl* (C=O, in aldehydes and ketones). Worked start: for an alkane with n = 3, CnH2n+2 gives C3H8 — propane.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Naming by chain length: CH4 methane (n=1), C2H6 ethane (n=2), C3H8 propane (n=3), C4H10 butane (n=4) — each fits CnH2n+2. Alkene check: ethene is C2H4, which fits CnH2n (n=2) and contains one C=C double bond. Functional groups in real molecules: ethanol, CH3CH2OH, carries a hydroxyl (-OH), so it is an alcohol; acetic acid, CH3COOH, carries a carboxyl (-COOH), so it is a carboxylic acid — the sour component of vinegar.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: (1) How many covalent bonds does a carbon atom form? (2) Give the molecular formula of the alkane with n = 5. (3) Which functional group defines an alcohol? (4) Ethene (C2H4) contains what kind of carbon–carbon bond? (5) Which family does CnH2n-2 describe? Answers: (1) four; (2) C5H12 (pentane); (3) hydroxyl, -OH; (4) a double bond (it's an alkene); (5) alkynes (triple bond).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: writing carbon with the wrong number of bonds — it always makes four. Mistake: confusing the family formulas — the ending shifts by two hydrogens each time (2n+2 alkane, 2n alkene, 2n-2 alkyne). Exit: (a) What functional group makes acetic acid an acid? (b) Is C3H6 an alkane or an alkene? Answers: the carboxyl group, -COOH; an alkene (it fits CnH2n).

items.translation: the minimum energy a collision needs for a reaction to occur
items.example: A catalyst speeds a reaction by lowering its activation energy.

items.translation: a substance that speeds a reaction without being consumed
items.example: The catalyst is regenerated, so it is left over at the end.

items.translation: the state where forward and reverse reaction rates are equal
items.example: At equilibrium the concentrations stay constant even though both reactions continue.

items.translation: a measure of acidity equal to -log[H+]
items.example: A [H+] of 1×10⁻³ M gives a pH of 3.

items.translation: the heat content of a system; ΔH is heat exchanged at constant pressure
items.example: An exothermic reaction has a negative ΔH because it releases heat.

items.translation: an atom cluster that gives an organic molecule its characteristic reactions
items.example: The carboxyl group (-COOH) makes acetic acid behave as an acid.

At 25 °C, pH + pOH equals…
questions.explanation: Because Kw = 1.0×10⁻¹⁴, pH + pOH = 14.

questions.explanation: The carboxyl group -COOH is the mark of a carboxylic acid.

questions.explanation: Exothermic reactions release heat and have ΔH < 0.

questions.prompt: Ethene, C2H4, contains a carbon–carbon…
questions.explanation: Fitting CnH2n, ethene is an alkene with one C=C double bond.

questions.explanation: pH above 7 is basic; pH 11 corresponds to [OH-] = 1×10⁻³ M.

lessons.title: Applied project: predict a reaction system

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Choose one industrially important reversible reaction (for example the Haber process, N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, or the contact process step 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3). You will not run it — you'll analyze it on paper the way a chemical engineer would, tying together balancing, kinetics, equilibrium, and energy.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) Write the balanced equation and confirm each element's atom count matches. 2) State whether it is exothermic or endothermic and what that means for ΔH's sign. 3) Name two conditions that would speed the reaction (kinetics) and explain why each works. 4) Use Le Chatelier's principle to predict how raising the pressure and raising the temperature each shift the equilibrium, and say which conditions maximize product yield. 5) Identify any acid, base, or organic product involved and, if an acid is present, show one pH calculation.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ The equation is balanced (atom counts verified on both sides). ✔ The ΔH sign is stated and justified. ✔ Two rate-increasing conditions are named with correct reasoning (temperature, concentration, surface area, or catalyst). ✔ The Le Chatelier predictions are correct, including counting gas moles for the pressure effect and treating heat as reactant/product for the temperature effect. ✔ Any pH calculation uses pH = -log[H+] correctly. If all five hold, you've reasoned through a real reaction system like a chemist.
